Astro: dictation for how bilingual people talk

Push-to-talk dictation for macOS that runs entirely on the laptop and copes with Hindi and English (or Gujarati and English) in the same sentence. It is a fork of the open-source app Handy.

The problem

Mainstream dictation picks one language per utterance. If you say a Hinglish sentence, it either mangles the Hindi or swaps scripts halfway through. Cloud tools also want your audio, and I did not want that.

So Astro keeps everything on the machine and measures itself on the case it exists for. Generic word error rate would not say much here, because Hindi can be written in Devanagari or in Roman letters and both are right. The benchmark has to fix a spelling policy first.

How it works

  1. Hold the shortcut and speak.The Rust core of the Tauri app records and cuts silence.
  2. Send it to a local backend.Models run as small Python HTTP services on the same machine. Backends are pluggable and the app checks that whatever answers is really Astro's server.
  3. Transcribe with Gemma 4.The shipping backend is Gemma 4 E4B with its language decoder quantized to 4 bits for Apple Silicon.
  4. Paste at the cursor.The text lands in whatever app you were typing in. No audio, screenshot or text leaves the Mac.
  5. Score against a fixed policy.A code-switch-aware scorer follows a written orthography policy. It refuses to publish a word error rate until human reference transcripts exist.

Results

This is a reference-free comparison, so it measures how consistent each model is about spelling, how fast it is and how much memory it takes. It does not measure accuracy.

Source: eval/results/codeswitch_bench_incumbent.md, run on-device with n = 76 clips. Parakeet's policy purity is an artifact: it wrote Latin script on 69 of 76 clips, never wrote Devanagari and returned nothing on 7, so the report ranks it out.

By the report's own sort order (cross-script word flips, then purity) Gemma is 4th of 5. Its 13 flips come from 2 clips where it wrote Devanagari. On the other 74 it wrote Roman Hindi, and it leads on policy purity.

Limits and next steps

  • There is no word error rate anywhere on this page. The 631 clips have no human transcripts yet, and the harness blocks a WER until they exist.
  • The benchmark covers 76 of those clips from one speaker. Nothing here says how it does for another voice or a noisy room.
  • The Gemma row cannot be reproduced by anyone else, because it is my own local 4-bit quantization and the weights are unpublished.
  • Latencies are file-in, text-out on warmed models, not the full press-to-paste path.
  • Next: record the hand-transcribed gold set, then try a LoRA fine-tune of the decoder on the lexemes that flip between scripts.
